Treasure Island Dizzy (NES) was the earliest game to make me legitimately angry.

Critics consider this one of the most difficult Dizzy games as the energy bar system of later titles was not yet implemented and Dizzy is provided with only one life—contrasting with five in the first game and three in Fantasy World Dizzy, the immediate sequel, and most subsequent titles. Also unique to this game, the player is unable to select any particular item from the inventory for use—Dizzy simply puts down whichever item is at the top of the list. If Dizzy is underwater and the snorkel happens to be at the top of the inventory list, he will drop the snorkel when the player collects another item and instantly die. Treasure Island Dizzy therefore requires more foresight and planning than the other games in the series.

Adding to the difficulty of the game was the fact that the player had two main tasks to complete; the escape from the islands, and the collection of the thirty coins. Indeed, upon escaping the final island, the Shopkeeper character appears and tells Dizzy that he cannot leave without finding all thirty coins. Given that a number of the coins were hidden behind scenery, this second task proved to be more difficult than the main game. Commodore Format printed a "complete" solution and map which did not include the hidden coins, frustrating many players.

Honorable mentions would be Bubsy in Close Encounters of the Furred Kind (SNES) and Taz in Escape From Mars (Sega Genesis)

  • Background stuff doesn't get in your way, unless it's a torch or something, then it counts as touching an open flame and you die.
  • You use an item by letting it fall off the top of your list, unless it's the pogo stick, at which case you gotta just hold it while you jump. Except, no, only when you jump in a very specific location.

The multiplayer in Doom is bland and boring, but not terrible. It's just generic, but not badly done. Nothing is broken and it's not particularly difficult to play because of any technical issues. Honestly, it's unsurprising. Doom was never really about multiplayer to being with. SP and the mod scene are the big draws for the original Doom games, not the multiplayer stuff. It was nice it was there, but that's not why it became what it is. On top of that, ID farmed the MP for the new Doom out to the dev that worked on the remastered Halo and CoD Ghosts.

It's there to check a feature off on the checklist of stuff shooters are expected to have and nothing more. I'm pretty sure they're satisfied with it just not sucking, and it doesn't, but it doesn't do any more than that either.

Well, that and to extend the use for the Snap Map feature. The map editor is the only real distinctive feature the MP has going for it, and even that will probably see more than it's fair share of SP and Co-op use as it supports both of those as well.

Half-Life, Half-Life 2, Half-Life 2 Episode 2.

But wait, I'll explain why I consider these games (all within opinion, of course) to be bad! The first in the franchise ended up having counter-intuitive confusing level design and awful platforming segments in a first-person-shooter type game, while the second had an underwhelming extremely linear path laid out specifically for the player with physics "puzzles" (yes, this was a selling point) that barely went beyond the scope of using bricks as a counter-lever or boulders to obstruct Antlion entrances, while Episode 2 ended with an incredibly frustrating and bland wave shooter where you defend a base from an onslaught of enemies that goes on for far too long.

tl;dr: I didn't like them. There are (obviously) worse games than the Half-Life franchise, but after playing other FPS's, that let me down.
Car Alarms Don't Work. Why Are They So Common?

Car theft was deeply embedded in Winnipeg’s teen culture. Peers pressured each other to steal cars, usually for joyriding. Thieves were quite young, stealing their first cars, on average, at age 13. There were even reports of 10-year-olds stealing cars with screwdrivers. “Auto theft is an activity for them,” one government informant explained in a report funded by Canada’s National Crime Prevention Centre. “Somehow it got started, and now it’s just what they do. In one neighborhood, they play pickup hockey. In this neighborhood, they steal cars.”
